q: Why install software with apt rather than a .deb found on a website?
choices: apt checks signatures and brings its updates later
explain: apt installs from repositories whose packages are signed, so it can tell they weren't tampered with, and apt upgrade brings their security fixes later. A .deb downloaded by hand never updates itself: it stays at that version, holes included, unless its site also offers an apt repository. If you must, apt install ./file.deb at least pulls its dependencies.

q: A security fix came out, but `apt upgrade` sees nothing new. What did you forget?
choices: apt update, to refresh the package lists
explain: apt keeps a local copy of the list of packages each repository offers. apt update downloads a fresh copy of those lists; it installs nothing. apt upgrade then compares that list with what you have. Without update, it compares against an old list and sees no new version. Always: apt update, then apt upgrade.

q: Which updates does a Debian stable server receive?
choices: Security and bug fixes, rarely new features
explain: On Debian stable, a package keeps the same version for the life of the release; only security and important bug fixes are added. Nothing changes behaviour under your feet, which is why servers use it. testing and unstable (sid) receive new versions every day: great for trying things, risky for a server.

q: Where do you look to see which repositories a server trusts?
explain: apt reads its repositories from /etc/apt/sources.list and from every file in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ (.list or the newer .sources files). Each repository there can install and run code as root on the machine, so a line you can't explain deserves a question. /etc/yum.repos.d/ is the Red Hat equivalent.

q: How do you see which packages have an update waiting?
explain: After apt update has refreshed the lists, apt list --upgradable shows each package with a newer version waiting, and both versions. Nothing is installed. Useful before a maintenance window: you know what is going to change, and you can spot a big one (kernel, database) that needs care.

q: You uninstall a service and want no config left behind. Which command?
explain: apt remove takes away the program but leaves its configuration files in /etc, so reinstalling it later finds your settings. apt purge removes those configuration files too. Your own data (a database's files in /var/lib, for example) may still stay: check before you reuse the machine.

q: You need a tool but don't know its package name. What do you run?
explain: apt search word looks for the word in every package's name and description, so it finds a package even when its name isn't the tool's name. Then apt show name gives its description, version and dependencies before you install. dpkg -S does something else: it tells which installed package owns a file.

q: How do you check whether nginx is installed, and which version?
explain: dpkg -l nginx asks the database of installed packages. The line starts with a two-letter status: ii means installed and fine, rc means removed but its config remains. The version column follows. ls /etc/nginx proves little: that folder can stay after apt remove.

q: apt asks 'Do you want to continue? [Y/n]'. What do you read before Y?
explain: To solve a conflict, apt sometimes decides to remove packages, and it lists them under 'The following packages will be REMOVED'. That list may contain something your server needs. Read it every time; if it's long or surprising, answer n and find out why first.

q: What does `apt autoremove` remove?
choices: Packages installed as dependencies that nothing needs now
Packages you haven't used in a month
explain: apt remembers whether you asked for a package (manual) or it came in as a dependency (auto). autoremove removes auto packages that nothing needs any more. Catch: a tool you use every day but that arrived as a dependency goes too. Read its list; apt-mark manual name keeps it. The download cache is emptied by apt clean, not this.

q: Security fixes should install even when nobody logs in for weeks. What do you set up?
choices: apt clean in a cron job
explain: unattended-upgrades downloads and installs security updates by itself every day, with no one logged in. A holey server you forget to update is how most break-ins happen, so on a machine you rarely visit it's the first thing to turn on. A weekly reboot installs nothing by itself.

q: How do you see what `apt remove name` would do, without doing it?
explain: -s (or --simulate) makes apt print everything it would do (install, upgrade, remove) and stop there, changing nothing. You see if removing one package would also drag others away. Good habit before any removal on a production server, and in scripts you are testing.

q: A new version of a package breaks your app. How do you keep upgrades off it?
explain: apt-mark hold name freezes the package at its current version: upgrades skip it, and apt-mark showhold lists what is held. The price: it also misses its security fixes. Write down why you held it, fix the real problem, then apt-mark unhold name.

q: Why turn on unattended-upgrades on a server?
choices: Security fixes land within a day, even if nobody logs in
It upgrades to the next Debian release
explain: Security holes are exploited within days of being published. unattended-upgrades installs the fixes daily even when nobody logs in, so the window stays short. Its settings are in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades, and what it did each day is in /var/log/unattended-upgrades/. It never moves you to the next Debian release.

q: Something broke overnight. Where do you see what apt installed or upgraded, and when?
explain: apt writes every run to /var/log/apt/history.log: the date, the command that ran, and each package with its old and new version. Compare those times with when the problem started. /var/log/dpkg.log gives every step in detail, and older logs are compressed next to them (.gz, read with zless).

q: You set the wrong timezone at install. How do you ask the package's questions again?
explain: Some packages ask questions when installed: timezone, language, keyboard. dpkg-reconfigure name asks them again and applies the new answers. Reinstalling doesn't ask again, since the answers are remembered, and editing dpkg's own files by hand can break the package database.

q: What does a repository's signature protect you from?
choices: A mirror or attacker serving modified packages
Bad code written by the publisher
explain: The publisher signs the repository with its key, and apt checks the signature before trusting any package. If a mirror, a proxy or an attacker changes a package on the way, the signature no longer matches and apt refuses it. It proves who published it and that it is intact, not that the code is good: only add publishers you trust.

q: Why not install a few packages from testing on a stable server?
choices: They pull newer libraries under the whole system
explain: A package from testing often needs newer libraries, and apt installs them too, under every other program of the system. You end up with a mix of releases nobody tested together (Debian calls it a FrankenDebian) that breaks at the next upgrade. Prefer the backports repository, made for stable, or run the new version in a container.

q: How do you check that installed files still match their packages?
explain: Each package ships a checksum for every file it installs. dpkg --verify (or debsums -c) recomputes them and lists the files that changed since installation. Config files in /etc change normally. A modified program in /usr/bin or /usr/sbin is a warning sign that someone may have replaced it.

q: `apt upgrade` leaves some packages 'kept back'. What does `apt full-upgrade` allow that upgrade doesn't?
choices: Removing packages to finish the upgrade
explain: apt upgrade never removes a package, so an update that needs to swap one package for another stays 'kept back'. apt full-upgrade may remove or replace packages to finish the job: that's what moving to a new Debian release needs. Read its removal list before saying yes.

q: A package installed a service. How do you find its files, config included?
explain: dpkg -L name lists every file the package put on disk: programs, config under /etc, the systemd unit, the docs. Much quicker and more exact than searching the whole disk with find. dpkg -S does the reverse: give it a file, it tells you the package.

q: unattended-upgrades is installed. Which command turns it on?
explain: Installing unattended-upgrades isn't enough: it must be switched on. dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades asks 'Automatically download and install stable updates?' and, on yes, writes /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades with the two daily settings set to "1": refresh the lists, and run the upgrade.

q: Out of the box on Debian, what does unattended-upgrades install?
choices: Updates from the security archive only
explain: By default it only takes packages from Debian's security archive, the ones that fix known holes. Other updates wait for you to install them by hand, when you can watch. The list of allowed origins is Origins-Pattern in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades. Security only is the careful choice.

q: How do you see what unattended-upgrades would do, without installing anything?
explain: --dry-run goes through the whole process without installing anything, and --debug explains each decision: which packages it would take and why others are skipped. Handy right after changing its settings. Afterwards, what it really did each day is in /var/log/unattended-upgrades/.

q: Which command shows a package's candidate version and where it comes from?
explain: apt policy name shows the installed version, the candidate (the one apt would install), and every repository offering the package with its priority. When two repositories offer it, the highest priority wins. This is how you understand why apt picks a version from backports or from a third-party repository.

q: You add a repository of your own. How do you make apt trust its packages?
choices: Save its key in /etc/apt/keyrings, cited by Signed-By
Run apt-key add, still the way today
Write trusted=yes in the sources entry
Nothing: apt trusts any repository you add
explain: Save the publisher's public key as a file in /etc/apt/keyrings/ and add Signed-By: pointing to it in that repository's entry. apt then accepts that key only for that repository, not for all of them. apt-key, which trusted a key everywhere, is gone; trusted=yes simply turns the check off.

q: `apt update` says NO_PUBKEY. What does it mean?
choices: apt has no key for that repository, so it won't trust it
The package list is corrupted, run apt clean
explain: NO_PUBKEY followed by an id means the repository is signed with a key apt doesn't have, so apt ignores it: it isn't broken, it's being careful. Fetch the key from the publisher's official site, convert it with gpg --dearmor into /etc/apt/keyrings/, and name it with Signed-By in the repository entry.

q: What does `update-alternatives --config editor` do?
choices: Chooses which program the editor link points to
Sets the EDITOR variable for your shell
Lists the editors in the repositories
explain: Some commands can be provided by several programs: editor can be nano or vim, java several JDKs. Debian keeps a link (/usr/bin/editor) pointing to the chosen one. update-alternatives --config editor shows the choices and switches the link for the whole system. Your own EDITOR variable still wins for you.

q: After upgrading openssl, which tool tells you which services still run the old one?
explain: A running program loaded the library when it started and keeps that old copy in memory. The file on disk is fixed, but the service is still vulnerable until it restarts. needrestart lists those services and offers to restart them. After a kernel update, only a reboot helps.

q: A file appeared in /usr/bin and you wonder where it came from. Which command tells you?
explain: dpkg -S /usr/bin/name searches the installed packages for that path and prints the package that owns it. If no package owns it, someone put it there by hand: a script, another admin, or an intruder. Worth finding out which. apt-file search does the same for packages you haven't installed.

q: What does `apt-mark auto name` change?
choices: It counts as a dependency: autoremove may take it
The package is held at its version
The package is reinstalled at the next boot
explain: apt-mark auto marks the package as if it had only come in as a dependency. Once nothing depends on it any more, apt autoremove will remove it. apt-mark manual does the opposite and protects it; apt-mark showauto and showmanual list each group.

q: Where do you write a pin to prefer one release for a package?
explain: Pinning lives in a file of /etc/apt/preferences.d/: one block with Package: (which package), Pin: (which release or version) and Pin-Priority: (how much to prefer it). sources.list only says where packages come from, not which to prefer. Check the result with apt policy name.

q: An upgrade stopped half way: which command finishes configuring the packages?
explain: When an upgrade is cut (lost connection, power, Ctrl+C), packages stay unpacked but not configured, and apt complains. dpkg --configure -a finishes configuring everything that was left half done. If dependencies are missing too, apt --fix-broken install is the next step.

q: After changing a kernel module or a crypttab entry, what do you rebuild?
choices: The package cache, with apt clean
explain: The initramfs is a small image the kernel loads at boot, with the modules and settings needed to reach the real disk (an encrypted disk, for example). If you change what boot needs, rebuild it with update-initramfs -u, or the machine may not find its disk at the next boot.

q: Which timers run apt's automatic updates on a modern Debian?
explain: Two systemd timers do the work: apt-daily.timer refreshes the package lists, then apt-daily-upgrade.timer runs unattended-upgrades to install. systemctl list-timers 'apt*' shows when each last ran and runs next. The old /etc/cron.daily/apt script only steps aside when systemd is there.

q: A database must never be upgraded by itself. How do you keep automatic updates off it?
explain: List it in Unattended-Upgrade::Package-Blacklist in 50unattended-upgrades, or apt-mark hold it: automatic updates then skip that package while everything else keeps getting its fixes. Write down why, and upgrade it by hand in a planned window, with a backup. Stopping the timer would stop all security updates.

q: unattended-upgrades installed a new openssl and a new kernel. What is still true?
choices: Running services and the kernel keep the old code for now
The machine reboots by itself by default
The old files stay in use forever
explain: New files are on disk, but running services keep the old openssl in memory and the machine still runs the old kernel, until restarted. needrestart lists the services to restart, and the file /var/run/reboot-required appears when a reboot is needed. Automatic reboots are off by default: schedule one.
